questions.question: What is called Apocope and Anaptyxis explain with examples? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is called Apocope and Anaptyxis? Explain with examples.
  • Apocope: Loss of a sound or syllable at the end of a word.
  • Examples:
  • • photograph → photo
  • • memorandum → memo
  • Anaptyxis: Addition of a vowel between two consonants to ease pronunciation.
  • Examples:
  • • film → filum
  • • athlete → athalete

questions.question: Describe Fortunatov's law with examples. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe Fortunatov's Law with examples.
  • Fortunatov's Law states that in Sanskrit, an aspirated consonant loses its aspiration
  • when another aspirated consonant follows in the next syllable.
  • Examples:
  • • bhudh → budh
  • • Similar de-aspiration occurs to avoid two aspirates in succession.

questions.question: How the Aryan languages are classified into centum and satam groups? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• How are the Aryan languages classified into Centum and Satam groups?
  • The Indo-European (Aryan) languages are divided into Centum and Satam groups
  • based on the development of the original palatal consonants.
  • Centum Group
  • In these languages, the palatal consonants changed into velar sounds (k, g).
  • Examples:
  • • Latin
  • • Greek
  • • Celtic
  • • Germanic
  • The word for "hundred" in Latin is centum, pronounced with a "k" sound, hence the
  • name Centum.
  • Satam Group
  • In these languages, the palatal consonants changed into sibilant sounds (s, sh).
  • Examples:
  • • Sanskrit
  • • Avestan
  • • Persian
  • • Balto-Slavic languages

questions.question: Explain Verner's law with examples. / [CO3] [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain Verner's Law with examples.
  • Verner's Law was discovered by Karl Verner in 1875. It explains certain exceptions to
  • Grimm's Law in the Germanic languages.
  • Statement of the Law
  • According to Verner's Law, the voiceless fricatives produced by Grimm's Law became
  • voiced when the preceding syllable was not accented in Proto-Indo-European.
  • The changes are:
  • • f → b
  • • þ (th) → d
  • • h → g
  • • s → z
  • Examples
